item.title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Survey of qudit quantum information hardware demonstrates that multi-level d>2 architectures match the Hilbert space of 70 qubits using 24 qudits with d=8, achieving gate-depth reductions exceeding one order of magnitude in dedicated quantum simulations.

Grade 0.499 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik

Figure

Landscape of qudit implementations showing controllable qudit dimension d on the horizontal axis versus the number of interacting qudits n on the vertical axis across experimental platforms.

Asks

What is the current experimental state of the art in high-fidelity state preparation, control, measurement, and fault tolerance across diverse qudit platforms?

But

Increased spectral crowding, heightened sensitivity to phase decoherence, energy relaxation across higher levels, and elevated classical and quantum crosstalk.

Tools

trapped ions · superconducting circuits · solid-state nuclear spins · photonic circuits · neutral atoms

Abstract

Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

item.title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Code distance d≥21 achieves logical error rates below 10−10 per syndrome cycle. Architecture supports over 120,000 logical qubits on 100 mm × 100 mm chip under CMOS-compatible multiplexing constraints.

Grade 0.483 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera

Asks

How to design a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture that integrates rotated surface codes, coherent shuttling routing, wiring constraints, and fault-tolerant logical operations?

But

Numerical and analytical estimates based on experimentally demonstrated physical parameters; assumes CMOS multiplexing wiring efficiencies hold across 100 mm × 100 mm wafer-scale footprint.

Tools

rotated surface code · dense silicon spin qubits · coherent 1D spin shuttling lanes · CMOS-compatible multiplexed control routing

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below 10⁻¹⁰ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm × 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.

item.title: Reproducible distributions of energy-relaxation times in superconducting qubits from broadband SWAP spectroscopy
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Cumulative distribution of qubit quality factor Q=2πf01T1 pooled over a 2.7 GHz SWAP spectroscopy sweep is repeatable with median Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.03, within 1.4 times sampling floor, and reproducible across 4 thermal cycles spanning 326 days.

Grade 0.437 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Maximilien F. Debbas, Ana Valdés-Curiel, Ming-Han Chou, Haifeng Qiao, Shahriar Aghaeimeibodi, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, Loren J. Swenson

Figure

Quality factor spectra, CDFs, and percentile drift across 8 sweeps repeated every 9 hours over 3 days for zero bandwidth, 50 MHz bandwidth, and 2.7 GHz bandwidth. Only broadband sweeps achieve tightly overlapping CDFs and a median spread of 0.07 M (6%).

Asks

Can sweeping qubit frequency over a broad bandwidth yield an energy-relaxation metric whose distribution is stationary and reproducible in time?

Before

Repeated single-frequency T1 inversion recovery had median Q spread of 1.54 M (74%) and median Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance 0.57 over 3 days.

But

Fit quality threshold χr2<3 required. Reproducibility shifts when strongly coupled TLS defects reshuffle or leave sweep bandwidth after thermal cycling.

Tools

fast-flux-assisted (FFA) SWAP spectroscopy · aluminum-on-silicon flux-tunable transmon qubits · two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance · permutation test

Abstract

The distribution of the qubit energy-relaxation time (T1) in a superconducting quantum processor affects its logical error rates. However, reports on qubit fabrication quality focus on the median or best-case T1 from measurements that are not reproducible due to resonant coupling to two-level system (TLS) defects whose frequencies fluctuate in time. Here, we sweep the frequency f01 of a flux-tunable qubit over several GHz with SWAP spectroscopy, quoting the quality factor Q = 2 pi f01 T1 to make T1 comparable across frequencies. We show that the cumulative distribution of Q pooled over the sweep is reproducible across four thermal cycles spanning 326 days, up to the reshuffling of strongly coupled TLSs. In contrast to repeated measurements at a single frequency, the medians of the broadband Q distributions spread by an order of magnitude less over 3 days. The distance between the cumulative distributions of repeats comes close to its sampling floor only for the broadband sweeps. The broadband Q distribution further resolves small coherence differences between identically designed qubits on two dies of the same wafer. These results establish the broadband Q distribution as a reproducible metric for qubit fabrication quality.

item.title: Real-Time Cryo-CMOS Photon-Number Readout from a Single SNSPD
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Cryo-CMOS logic at 4 K isolates single-photon events directly from intrinsic SNSPD signal timing with (13.9±0.3) ns latency, reducing heralded source g(2) by (24±5)%.

Grade 0.432 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play” · Niklas Lamberty, Dileep V. Reddy, Aishi Barua, Martin J. Stevens, Tim J. Bartley

Figure

Count rate and its derivative plotted against laser clock delay alongside rising-edge delay from a TDC, showing distinct single-photon and multi-photon timing plateaus preserved by the cryo-CMOS filter.

Asks

Can intrinsic photon-number resolution from a single SNSPD be extracted in real time inside a cryostat with low enough latency for feedforward operations?

Before

Similar cryogenic feedforward circuits reported electrical delays of (20±2) ns, while intrinsic photon-number resolution required room-temperature TDCs or oscilloscopes with high latency.

But

Discriminates only n=0,1, and 2+ photons; cannot distinguish n=2 from n≥3. Idler collection loss of roughly 64% limits g(2) suppression. Total dissipation is 12.8 mW.

Tools

packaged CMOS logic gates (NAND, SR-latch) at 4 K · high-inductance SNSPD at 1 K · type-II SPDC source

Abstract

Measurements leveraging the intrinsic photon-number resolution of Superconducting Nanostrip Single-Photon Detectors (SNSPDs) have recently gained traction due to the simplicity of the detector design. Intrinsic photon-number measurement schemes using SNSPDs encode the photon-number information in picosecond signal timing; these systems thus require high bandwidth readout and sensitive electrical measurement equipment. We show a cryogenic electronic circuit operating close to the SNSPD in the cryostat, which can isolate single-photon detection events directly from the SNSPD signal. This reduces the latency of the photon-number readout to (13.9 ± 0.3) ns, which enables feedforward operations based on intrinsic photon-number measurements with low latency.

item.title: Complementary mechanisms of critical quantum metrology
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Critical estimation of intrinsic parameter φ achieves δφ∼N−2/3 solely through suppressed quantum noise without enhanced response. This matches the δr∼N−2/3 scaling of parameter r, which is driven by diverging susceptibility despite increased noise.

Grade 0.430 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity quantum electrodynamics for superconducting electrical circuits: An arch…” · Nikita Leppenen, Shaked Levy, Ephraim Shahmoon

Figure

Plots (a)-(d) show estimation errors, N−2/3 finite-size scaling, noise/signal decompositions, and the N2/3 energy gap opening versus spin number N for the Ising ground state.

Asks

Can quantum noise suppression at criticality enhance the estimation of intrinsic system parameters without relying on enhanced susceptibility or external interferometric encoding?

Before

Standard quantum limit error scales as N−1/2; previous critical metrology achieved super-SQL scaling exclusively via enhanced susceptibility of order parameters.

But

Asymptotic to large spin counts N≫1; restricted to finite-size critical boundary r=rN∼1−(3/N)2/3 before mean-field transition softens.

Tools

coherently radiating spin states (CRSS) · driven-dissipative Dicke master equation · all-to-all transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian · exact numerical diagonalization

Abstract

Critical metrology conventionally exploits enhanced susceptibility to a system parameter near a phase transition. Here we identify a complementary mechanism for critically enhanced estimation of intrinsic system parameters via suppressed quantum noise rather than enhanced response. We demonstrate both mechanisms in coherently radiating spin states (CRSS)-correlated states of N spin-1/2 particles defined as asymptotic eigenstates of the collective-spin lowering operator with complex eigenvalue r e^(-iφ). At the critical value r=1, CRSS exhibit a second-order transition. We show that near criticality, estimation of r benefits from enhanced susceptibility despite increased noise, whereas estimation of φ benefits from suppressed quantum noise without enhanced response. Remarkably, both yield the same estimation error ∼N^(-2/3), improving over the standard quantum limit N^(-1/2). For φ, this establishes quantum-enhanced metrology of phases intrinsic to the critical system, rather than phases externally encoded by interferometry. We demonstrate these results for CRSS realizations in both dissipative (superradiant) and Hamiltonian (Ising) systems relevant to cavity QED and trapped ions, where fast preparation of CRSS is shown possible thanks to gap opening. Applications to metrology of coupling rates and phases or optical lengths are discussed.

item.title: Ancilla-Assisted Accelerated Readout of Transmon Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Correlating a target transmon with an ancilla transmon via CNOT gate doubles the resonator dispersive shift to χ1+χ2, reducing total measurement duration by a factor of approximately 0.6 while matching readout quality.

Grade 0.421 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Christopher Corlett, Noah Linden, Paul Skrzypczyk

Figure

Heat map of the total duration ratio (τ6(2)+τC)/τ6(1) across target and ancilla detunings Δ1 and Δ2. Values below 1 indicate measurement speed-up using the two-transmon scheme over the standard single-transmon readout.

Asks

Can dispersive readout of transmon qubits be accelerated without sacrificing measurement quality or moving outside the dispersive regime?

But

Numerical simulations. Assumes negative TR detunings, steady-state photon number nss=18, and negligible direct transmon-transmon coupling mediated by tunable couplers.

Tools

transmon-transmon-resonator (TTR) dispersive readout · Floquet branch analysis · Schrieffer-Wolff transformation · fast CNOT gate

Code. https://github.com/custal/ancilla-assisted-accelerated-readout-of-transmon-qubits

Abstract

We present a scheme for accelerating dispersive readout of superconducting transmon qubits. Dispersive readout works by weakly coupling the target transmon to a resonator, such that the resonator experiences a state-dependent frequency shift, which can then be read out. Our scheme introduces an ancillary transmon coupled to the same resonator. By appropriately correlating its state with that of the target transmon (using a fast CNOT gate), we show that the resonator frequency shift is approximately doubled, halving the required measurement duration to maintain the same quality. We present analytical results within the dispersive approximation, before employing and extending the recently introduced technique of branch analysis to account for ionization and other nonlinearities. Using this, and taking into account realistic noise and gate times, we show that our scheme allows measurement durations smaller by a factor of approximately 0.6, demonstrating that it offers a viable route for accelerating measurements of transmon qubits.

item.title: Phonon-Aware Electron-to-Nuclear Spin Quantum Memory in NV Centers
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Increasing spin-phonon coupling gph from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, oscillating with the 1/fm=1μs phonon period due to electron-phonon entanglement generated during write and partially undone during read.

Grade 0.415 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Manjith Baby Sarojam Chellam

Figure

Final memory fidelity as a function of nuclear-spin storage time up to 25μs for four values of spin-phonon coupling gph. Fidelity exhibits 1μs periodic revivals matching the phonon-mode period, with lower envelope dropping as gph increases.

Asks

How do phonon-induced relaxation, dephasing, and spin-phonon coupling during state transfer affect the fidelity of an electron-to-nuclear spin quantum memory in an NV center?

But

Numerical simulation with single effective phonon mode rather than continuum bath. Decoherence rates and spin-phonon coupling are phenomenological rather than fitted to experimental diamond data.

Tools

Lindblad master equation · QuTiP simulation · hyperfine-resonant drive in rotating frame · single-mode spin-phonon coupling model

Code. https://github.com/manjithbc/nv-quantum-memory

Abstract

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits. In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center. The model includes the NV electron spin, a coupled 13C nuclear spin, the hyperfine interaction, an effective microwave/radio-frequency-assisted SWAP interaction for writing and reading, a single effective phonon mode with longitudinal spin-phonon coupling, and Lindblad relaxation and dephasing channels. The dynamics are simulated with the Lindblad master equation in QuTiP, using the secular approximation and a hyperfine-resonant drive in the rotating frame. Without spin-phonon coupling and electron decoherence, the write-store-read protocol recovers the stored state with a fidelity above 0.9999. With the default decoherence rates, increasing the spin-phonon coupling from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers the worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, and the fidelity oscillates with the phonon-mode period because electron-phonon entanglement generated during the write step is partially undone during the read step. With a phenomenological temperature-dependent rate model, the fidelity decreases monotonically from 0.9997 at 1 K to 0.9938 at 300 K, while storage-time losses follow the assumed nuclear-spin decoherence rates. The storage-time plots, temperature sweep, and parameter maps identify operating regimes for NV-center quantum memory, and the accompanying open-source code provides a reproducible framework for studying phonon-limited quantum memory.

item.title: Localization of an Individual Charge Fluctuator in a Si/SiGe Spin Qubit Device
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Individual charge fluctuator localized to 1 nm by 31 nm laterally and 4 nm vertically (z=6 nm to 10 nm) within ALD Al2O3 bulk, with vertical dipole moment of 3 to 4 eA˚.

Grade 0.414 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Leah Tom, John Nichol, Chris Anderson, Mark F. Gyure

Figure

Spatial candidate positions and dipole moments matching experimental constraints; combining gate-referred shifts with 5 gate-TLF detuning lever arms isolates the defect to a 1 nm × 31 nm × 4 nm volume in the gate oxide.

Asks

Where are individual two-level charge fluctuators physically located within a semiconductor spin qubit device?

Before

Prior TLF localization methods relied solely on sensing-dot chemical potential shifts or inter-dot noise correlations, which leave dipole depth, orientation, and magnitude underconstrained.

But

Applied post-hoc to a single experimental TLF dataset; evaluated on candidate grid with excluded interfaces; higher sensitivity to vertically oriented than horizontally oriented dipoles.

Tools

self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson device simulations · RF reflectometry sensing-dot chemical potential shifts · gate-TLF detuning lever arm triangulation · detailed-balance switching rate analysis

Abstract

Charge noise from two-level fluctuators (TLFs) limits gate fidelities in semiconductor spin qubits, yet locating individual fluctuators within a device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a spatial triangulation method that combines the gate dependence of a TLF's detuning with the chemical potential shifts it induces in a sensing dot. Applying this method to previously reported measurements from a gated Si/SiGe quantum dot device, we use electrostatic simulations to jointly constrain the fluctuator's three-dimensional position and the magnitude of its electric dipole moment. We localize the fluctuator to a region spanning 31 nm by 1 nm laterally and 4 nm vertically within the bulk of the atomic layer deposited aluminum oxide, identifying the material hosting this individual charge-noise source. The measurements are consistent with a vertically oriented TLF with a magnitude of 3 to 4 emathringA. This approach provides a route to determining which materials and interfaces host active charge fluctuators in semiconductor spin qubit devices.
